Blue
blū
a. and n. (the colour of the heavens; a tabernacle colour; rendering Hebrew tekeleth)
From the Old French bleu, of Germanic origin. Hebrew tekeleth is a blue-violet dye, also obtained from a shellfish, and is the colour most associated with heaven — the pavement under God's feet in Exodus 24 is like a sapphire stone, as it were the body of heaven in his clearness.

Biblical Definition

Blue is a commanded colour of the sanctuary, and Scripture gives it a specific office: it is the colour of remembrance and of heavenly things. The high priest's robe was made entirely of it — “And thou shalt make the robe of the ephod all of blue” (Exodus 28:31) — and the golden plate on his mitre, engraved HOLINESS TO THE LORD, was fastened with “a blue lace, that it may be upon the mitre” (Exodus 28:37). Blue also carried the law into the daily dress of every Israelite, not merely the priest's: God commanded that they “make them fringes in the borders of their garments… and that they put upon the fringe of the borders a ribband of blue” (Numbers 15:38), and the stated purpose was memory — that ye may look upon it, and remember all the commandments of the LORD, and do them. It is the thread of a wearable catechism. When the camp moved, the ark was covered first with the veil, then with badgers' skins, and then “a cloth wholly of blue” (Numbers 4:6) — the most sacred object in Israel travelling under the colour of heaven, so that the marching camp saw a patch of sky moving in its midst.

Webster 1828 Definition

The blue-violet tekeleth of the sanctuary — the colour of the heavens. The high priest's robe was all of blue, and every Israelite wore a ribband of blue on his fringe to remember the commandments.

expand to see more

BLUE, a. [Fr. bleu.] One of the seven primary colors, being that of the clear sky.

2. As a noun, the color itself; also, blue cloth or dye.

3. In the tabernacle, one of the three commanded colors, with purple and scarlet.

4. Of the high priest's robe, made wholly of blue, Exod. 28.

5. In Scripture, a ribband of blue upon the fringe, for remembrance of the commandments, Num. 15.

Key Scripture

Exodus 28:31 — "And thou shalt make the robe of the ephod all of blue."

Numbers 15:38 — "Speak unto the children of Israel, and bid them that they make them fringes in the borders of their garments throughout their generations, and that they put upon the fringe of the borders a ribband of blue:"

Numbers 4:6 — "And shall put thereon the covering of badgers' skins, and shall spread over it a cloth wholly of blue, and shall put in the staves thereof."

Exodus 28:37 — "And thou shalt put it on a blue lace, that it may be upon the mitre; upon the forefront of the mitre it shall be."

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. What has been lost is the deliberate use of the visible to serve memory — God appointing a thread of colour so that a man would look, remember, and obey.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The instructive thing about Numbers 15:38 is how ordinary the mechanism is. God knows that his people forget, and rather than merely commanding them not to, he attaches a blue thread to the hem of every garment so that the reminder is in the corner of the eye all day. The text gives the reason plainly: that ye may look upon it, and remember all the commandments of the LORD, and do them, and that ye seek not after your own heart and your own eyes.

The principle to recover is not a fringe on the coat — the ceremonial law is fulfilled in Christ and its shadows are not to be reinstituted. It is the recognition that God accommodates our weak memories, and that he has appointed means for the same end under the new covenant: the reading and preaching of the word, the Lord's Supper as a remembrance, the Lord's Day itself recurring every seventh day. Our Lord's rebuke of the Pharisees for enlarging their borders shows the abuse to avoid, where a means of remembrance becomes a badge of display; but the abuse does not cancel the wisdom of appointed reminders.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tekeleth is blue-violet, a shellfish dye, and the sanctuary's heavenly colour; tsitsith is the fringe to which the blue ribband was fastened. Greek huakinthinos renders it in the Septuagint.

expand to see more

Hebrew tekeleth (H8504) — blue, violet; the colour of the high priest's robe and the ark's travelling cloth.

Hebrew tsitsith (H6734) — fringe, tassel; the border to which the ribband of blue was bound.

Hebrew pethil (H6616) — a cord, a lace, a ribband; the blue lace fastening the golden plate.

Hebrew sappir (H5601) — sapphire; the paved work under God's feet, as the body of heaven in clearness.

Greek huakinthinos (G5191) — of hyacinth colour, blue; the Septuagint's term for tekeleth.

Usage

"Of the high priest's robe: thou shalt make the robe of the ephod all of blue (Exodus 28:31)."

"Of a wearable reminder of the law: put upon the fringe of the borders a ribband of blue (Numbers 15:38)."

"Of the ark in transit: spread over it a cloth wholly of blue (Numbers 4:6)."
